indiaMissions/india-east-syriac-links/ti: Persian crosses, copper plates and the Church of the East in India
indiaMissions/india-east-syriac-links/pl: Kollam (Quilon), Kerala — site of the Tharisa church
indiaMissions/india-east-syriac-links/su: From late antiquity until 1599 the Christians of India belonged to the Church of the East, whose patriarch sat at Seleucia-Ctesiphon and later Baghdad. Bishops, liturgy and Syriac learning came from Mesopotamia and Persia along the sea routes of the Indian Ocean trade. Their traces survive in Pahlavi-inscribed 'Persian crosses', the Tharisappalli copper plates of 849, travellers' reports from Cosmas to Marco Polo, and letters between Kerala and the patriarchs that end only with the Portuguese-enforced break at Diamper.
indiaMissions/india-east-syriac-links/st:
The Church of the East grew up in the Persian (Sasanian) empire, outside the Roman world and its councils, and was the great missionary church of Asia, reaching Central Asia and Tang China by 635. India lay at the end of its maritime networks. A bishop styled 'John the Persian, of all Persia and Great India' is listed among those at Nicaea in 325, though the title's meaning is debated. The first reliable witness is the Alexandrian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes, who around 550 wrote that there were churches in Taprobane (Sri Lanka) served by Persian clergy, in “Male, where the pepper grows”, and at Kalliana (Kalyan near Mumbai), where a bishop was appointed from Persia.

India's place in the hierarchy changed over time. In the 650s the Catholicos Isho'yahb III rebuked the metropolitan of Fars, who claimed authority over India, for leaving the Indian churches without clergy. Under the great Catholicos Timothy I (780–823), India was organised as a metropolitan province of the 'exterior' provinces, whose metropolitan was required only to send a letter of communion every six years because of the distance. Syriac remained the language of liturgy and theology; Indian Christians used the East Syriac rite of Addai and Mari and called their bishops 'Mar'.

The richest documentary evidence is the set of copper plates known as the Tharisappalli or Quilon plates (c. 849). In them Ayyan Adikal Thiruvadikal, ruler of Venad under the Chera king Sthanu Ravi, granted land, serfs and trading rights to the church (palli) of Tharisa at Kollam, built by the merchant Maruvan Sapir Iso, and placed the church under the protection of the Anjuvannam and Manigramam merchant guilds. The plates are witnessed by eleven signatories in Arabic (Kufic), ten in Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and four in Judeo-Persian (Hebrew script) — vivid proof of a cosmopolitan Indian Ocean trading world. Later plates, such as the Iravi Korttan grant at Kodungallur (traditionally dated 1225; the date is debated), show Christian merchants holding guild titles. The so-called Persian crosses — granite slabs carved with a cross rising from a lotus beneath a dove and bearing Pahlavi inscriptions — have been found at St Thomas Mount near Chennai (unearthed by the Portuguese in 1547), in the Valiyapalli at Kottayam (two crosses), at Kadamattom, Muttuchira and Alangad in Kerala, at Agassaim in Goa (2001) and at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka. Scholars date them between the seventh and tenth centuries; one common reading of the inscription asks the Lord Christ to have mercy on the man who made the cross.

Western visitors came intermittently. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that King Alfred sent alms to St Thomas in India in 883, though the destination may be legendary. Marco Polo described the tomb of Thomas at Mylapore in about 1293. The Franciscan John of Montecorvino spent thirteen months there in 1291–92 on his way to China; the Dominican Jordanus Catalani was appointed Latin bishop of Columbum (Kollam) in 1329; and the papal legate Giovanni de' Marignolli worshipped at a Latin church in Kollam in 1348. These Latin contacts left little lasting trace, and the Indian church continued to look to Mesopotamia.

By the fifteenth century the Church of the East had been devastated in its homeland by plague, Timur's campaigns and decline, and India sometimes went decades without bishops. In 1490 Kerala sent three men to the Catholicos Shemon IV, who consecrated two monks, Mar Thomas and Mar John, for India. In 1503 Elijah V sent four more — Mar Yahballaha, Mar Denha, Mar Jacob and Mar Thomas — whose letter of 1504 reported about 30,000 Christian families and the newly arrived Portuguese. Mar Jacob (d. c. 1552) cooperated closely with the Portuguese at Cranganore. After the 1552 schism in Mesopotamia created a rival Chaldean patriarchate in communion with Rome, both lines sent bishops: Mar Joseph Sulaqa (d. 1569) and Mar Abraham (d. 1597), who manoeuvred between the patriarchs, Rome and the Portuguese. The Portuguese increasingly intercepted East Syriac bishops at sea. Mar Abraham's death in 1597 gave Archbishop Menezes of Goa the opportunity to end the connection at the Synod of Diamper in 1599. Thereafter only a small Chaldean Syrian Church in Thrissur (re-linked to the Assyrian patriarch from 1874 and organised under Mar Abimalek Timotheus from 1908) continued the East Syriac affiliation, while the Syro-Malabar Church kept the East Syriac rite in a Latinised form within the Catholic Church.

indiaMissions/india-east-syriac-links/le: The East Syriac connection shows that Indian Christianity was part of an Asian Christian world centred on Baghdad long before Europeans arrived. Its material remains — the Pahlavi crosses and multilingual copper plates — are among the best evidence for the cosmopolitan Indian Ocean of the ninth century, and its liturgical heritage became the focus of twentieth-century efforts to undo Latinisation.

indiaMissions/india-portuguese-padroado/: Portuguese Padroado, Goa and the Goa Inquisition
Old Goa (Velha Goa)

Under the Padroado Real, papal bulls of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries gave the Portuguese crown the right and duty to fund, staff and govern the Catholic Church throughout its eastern empire. From the conquest of Goa in 1510 Portuguese India became a Catholic territory: temples were destroyed, Hindu rites restricted, orphans baptised, and from 1560 the Goa Inquisition policed converts until 1812. The same system produced India's first printing press, Konkani and Marathi Christian literature, a large Goan and Mangalorean Catholic community and a long jurisdictional quarrel with Rome.

The Padroado (patronage) grew out of papal bulls such as Romanus Pontifex (1455), Inter caetera (1456) and Praecelsae devotionis (1514), which granted the kings of Portugal control of church appointments and revenues in lands they 'discovered' in return for supporting missions. When Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, and Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, church and empire advanced together. Franciscans accompanied the early fleets and opened a friary in Goa in 1517; Goa became a diocese in 1534 and an archdiocese, with the title 'Primate of the East', in 1558. Dominicans (1548), Jesuits (1542), Augustinians (1572) and later Carmelites and Theatines followed. Cochin (1558) and Cranganore became suffragan sees; the see of Mylapore (San Thome) was created in 1606.

In the 1540s the colonial state turned from tolerance to active Christianisation in its core territories of Tiswadi (Ilhas), Bardez and Salcete. Temples on the islands were ordered destroyed in 1540–41 and their lands transferred to churches and the Confraternity of the Holy Faith (1541); the College of St Paul trained boys of many Asian nations. Viceregal and conciliar decrees between 1559 and 1567 — including the 1559 law that Hindu children left fatherless were to be handed to the Jesuits for baptism, bans on public Hindu worship and festivals, the expulsion of Brahmin priests and preference in office for Christians — produced mass baptisms, often of entire villages following their headmen. Many Hindu families fled across the border, carrying their deities to new temples in Ponda and beyond. The First Provincial Council of Goa (1567) codified this policy. By the early seventeenth century the majority of the population of the 'Old Conquests' was Catholic, while caste survived among converts as Bamonn (Brahmin), Chardo (Kshatriya), Gauddo and Sudir groups.

Francis Xavier, writing to King João III in 1545, asked for an Inquisition; it was established in Goa in 1560. Its first target was New Christians — converted Jews and their descendants, such as the physician Garcia de Orta, whose remains were exhumed and burned in 1580 — but it increasingly prosecuted Hindu converts suspected of continuing ancestral rites, and even regulated Hindu practice in Portuguese lands. Contemporary and later accounts, notably the French physician Charles Dellon's narrative of his imprisonment (1687), made it notorious in Europe. Historians estimate that some 16,000 people were tried between 1561 and 1774, with dozens burned in person or in effigy. The Marquis of Pombal suppressed it in 1774; it was restored in 1778 and finally abolished in 1812, and most of its archive was destroyed.

The Padroado also sustained real cultural achievement. The first printing press in India was set up at the College of St Paul in 1556. The English Jesuit Thomas Stephens wrote a Konkani grammar and the Kristapurana (printed 1616), an epic retelling of the Bible in the Marathi-Konkani of Hindu puranic poetry; Jesuit and Franciscan scholars produced grammars, catechisms and dictionaries in Konkani, Marathi and Tamil. The Rachol Seminary (from 1610) trained Goan clergy, and Goan priests such as Joseph Vaz, who secretly rebuilt the Catholic church of Dutch-ruled Ceylon from 1687, became missionaries in their own right. Portuguese enclaves at Bassein, Chaul, Bombay, Daman, Diu, Mangalore, Nagapattinam and Hooghly left lasting Catholic communities such as the East Indians of Bombay and the Mangalorean Catholics.

The Padroado's claims soon collided with Rome. In 1622 the papacy founded the Congregation de Propaganda Fide to take direct control of missions, and from 1637 it appointed vicars apostolic in India — beginning with the Goan Brahmin Matheus de Castro, the first Indian bishop — in territories Portugal claimed but could no longer control. The resulting 'double jurisdiction' produced rival priests, excommunications and, in the nineteenth century, the 'Goan schism' after Pope Gregory XVI's brief Multa praeclare (1838) suppressed Padroado sees outside Portuguese territory. Concordats in 1857 and 1886 created a compromise hierarchy, and the Padroado in India was wound down after 1928 and ended after India annexed Goa in 1961. Meanwhile Mangalorean Catholics suffered captivity under Tipu Sultan, who deported tens of thousands to Seringapatam in 1784; many died before their release in 1799.

The Padroado's legacy is double-edged. It planted a large, culturally distinct Catholic population on India's west coast and supplied the subcontinent with priests, musicians, teachers and administrators. It also made Christianity in India look like the religion of the conqueror — 'Parangi' (Firangi) religion — associating it with temple destruction, forced baptism and inquisitorial terror, memories that Hindu nationalist writers have revived. In the 2011 census Goa's 366,130 Christians formed about 25 per cent of the state's population.

The Padroado created the oldest Latin Catholic communities of India and gave the west coast a distinctive Indo-Portuguese Christian culture of churches, music and cuisine. It is also the clearest Indian example of mission fused with colonial power: temple destruction, coerced baptism and the Inquisition remain central to debates about conversion in India, and Rome's struggle to free the church from royal patronage foreshadowed the later push for an Indian-led hierarchy.
